A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StableToken research. All 24 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison. Relocated related work and renumbered reconstruction results can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original tokenizer robustness, reconstruction, downstream ASR/SER/TTS, and ablation results in Tables 1–6, Figure 3, and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds efficiency benchmarks, token-distribution analyses, boundary-stability measurements, and architectural ablations in Tables 13–20.

M1.justification: The Voting-LFQ architecture, bit-wise aggregation, consensus training, and combined objective remain unchanged. The new architectural variants are ablations. Appendix B.8 presents 30-second processing and chunking as clarification of existing behavior, rather than a revised inference method.

E1.justification: Table 20 adds ASR evaluation on WenetSpeech and KeSpeech, while Appendix B.7 analyzes token distributions using LibriSpeech and AISHELL. This extends evaluation coverage within the existing speech tasks and bilingual scope; the training dataset lists are substantively retained.

E2.justification: v1's efficiency analysis compares StableToken voter-count configurations. v2 additionally evaluates GLM-4-Voice-Tokenizer against StableToken in the hardware benchmarks of Tables 13–14. Comparator membership in the retained robustness, reconstruction, and downstream experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols cover CPU/GPU latency, RTF, throughput, and memory across four batch-duration combinations; vocabulary utilization, entropy, and KL divergence; regional UED using 15%/70%/15% temporal partitions; and architectural comparisons at 100k training steps. These substantially broaden measurement procedures without revising the retained benchmark settings.

E4.justification: v2 retains the component and voter-count ablations and adds quantizer-depth and clean/noisy-ratio ablations in Appendix C. Appendices B.6–B.8 additionally investigate practical efficiency, bilingual codebook utilization and specialization, and whether noise-induced token inconsistencies concentrate near audio boundaries.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added token frequencies, entropy, and KL values are descriptive measurements, not a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Retained results match, including average UED 10.17% and v1 Table 16's reconstruction results in v2 Table 24. Tables 13–20 add substantial new findings. For example, Table 20 reports UED 18.68% versus 13.65% but SER accuracy 67.38% versus 59.51% for Layer 16 versus Layer 24 at 100k steps. These are new ablation comparisons, not version-to-version performance changes.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and their mathematical reasoning remain unchanged. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or guarantee is introduced. Entropy and KL divergence are used as empirical analysis metrics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific contributions: identifying tokenizer instability, introducing voting and consensus training, improving token robustness while preserving reconstruction quality, and benefiting downstream SpeechLLMs. The new experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations linking memory savings to LFQ, token distributions to language-specific phonetic specialization, and boundary measurements to chunking suitability. Appendix C explains quantizer depth through a robustness-versus-acoustic-detail tradeoff and hypothesizes that more perturbed branches strengthen invariant learning. These extend v1's mechanism and applicability discussion considerably.

D1.justification: v2 documents the 3:2 clean/noisy configuration, 30-second training truncation, independent inference chunks and concatenation, and benchmark hardware. Its abstract also supplies a repository link and states that code and models are public, although the reproducibility statement retains the earlier promise of release upon acceptance. Actual availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: The expanded Section 5 largely relocates v1 Appendix G, including its discussion of R-SPIN, NAST, and acoustic-tokenizer consistency. Research positioning is retained. Changes to TESS, VCTK, and other bibliography entries update metadata for the same cited resources rather than introduce new related work.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammatical and terminology corrections, updates affiliations and conference headers, and adds acknowledgments. It consolidates the detailed related work into Section 5, subdivides Appendix B.6, and reorganizes appendix labels. The existing method and results narrative is largely preserved.

P2.justification: New tables substantially expand the displayed evidence: grouped CPU/GPU measurements, bilingual vocabulary and frequency summaries, KL divergence, temporal error distributions, and multitask architectural ablations in Tables 13–20. Existing figures and benchmark tables remain, while later appendix tables are relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The hardware measurements supplement v1's FLOP-based efficiency argument, and Table 20 provides useful evidence for configuration choices while exposing a robustness/SER tradeoff. Added processing details also improve clarity. These strengthen an already extensively evaluated paper, but uncertainty reporting remains absent, boundary measurements only indirectly support long-audio claims, and release statements are inconsistent. The net gain is positive but limited.
